subject: Architecture
title: The Hyatt Regency Walkway: Design Error
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Hyatt Regency Walkway: Design Error usable.

hook.text: In 1981, two elevated walkways in a Kansas City hotel collapsed during a dance party, killing 114.

buildup.text: The original design used a single rod connecting both walkways to the ceiling. It passed engineering review.

discovery.text: During construction, the rod was split into two segments. This doubled the load on the upper connection.

twist.text: The change looked minor on paper. In reality, it made the connection too weak to hold the weight above.

climax.text: The disaster changed engineering ethics — reviews of construction changes became mandatory industry-wide.

punchline.text: A small change on a drawing. The deadliest structural failure in U.S. history.

quiz.question: What caused the Hyatt Regency walkway collapse?
options: An earthquake shook the building during the event
A construction change doubled the load on a connection point
Too many people stood on the walkway at once

details.summary: On July 17, 1981, two suspended walkways in the Hyatt Regency Kansas City hotel collapsed during a tea dance, killing 114 people. A seemingly minor design change — splitting one long hanger rod into two shorter ones — doubled the load on a critical connection, causing catastrophic failure.
details.whyItMatters: The Hyatt Regency disaster is engineering's most-studied structural failure. It demonstrated that small design changes can have catastrophic consequences and permanently changed how structural engineers review and approve construction modifications.
takeaways: 114 people died when two suspended walkways collapsed in 1981
A minor design change doubled the load on a critical connection
It transformed engineering review and approval processes

faq.question: What was the design change that caused the collapse?
faq.answer: The original design used one continuous rod from ceiling to lower walkway. The built design split this into two rods, requiring the upper walkway connection to support both walkways' weight. This doubled the load on a nut-and-washer connection that was already at its limit.

faq.question: What changed in engineering practice after the disaster?
faq.answer: Engineers of record became responsible for reviewing all field changes. The incident is now a core ethics case study in engineering education. The two responsible engineers lost their licenses. Professional liability insurance requirements and peer review processes were strengthened nationwide.
